initial_requirements: The Federal Highway Administration needs the Clarus system to collect, quality-control, and share environmental and road-condition observations from transportation networks. Transportation agencies, observation-system operators, weather-service providers, and researchers should be able to contribute or use the data. The system is intended to support safer road operations, timely responses to weather, and improved forecasting through an integrated source of surface transportation observations.

slots.key: Publication rules for approved observations
slots.value: Approved observations must be timely, usable, traceable, and trusted enough by operational users to support decisions; downstream users should be able to find them and understand their context. Core observation flow should be stable, with quality control applied to contributor data and clear context for use. A research observation can be labeled usable for operations if it has been checked against Clarus quality rules and the source and method are reasonably clear; if method or quality cannot be fully verified, it should still be accepted but marked as informational or experimental so users do not rely on it the same way. At minimum, users should see where it came from, when it was collected, what kind of observation it is, and any validation status or limitations known; if provenance is incomplete, that uncertainty should be visible. Research-derived observations that are not vetted to the same standard as an operational feed must be explicitly marked as research-only or experimental. They should only be treated as operationally usable when the source, method, and quality controls are known and they have passed Clarus validation for routine use. The record should show the source type, collection method if known, validation status, and any limitations or caveats so users can immediately tell it did not come from a standard sensor feed unless it has been elevated to that level. Search and visualization must respect the same access restrictions as the underlying observations, and results should clearly label estimated, stale, incomplete, flagged, low-confidence, unverified, aggregated, or derived views so they are not mistaken for confirmed ground truth. These states should be made obvious with a visible label and, where possible, a simple status indicator right in the result row or map view, not hidden in a field or download.

slots.key: Data-sharing restrictions by source sensitivity and contributor agreement
slots.value: Restrictions should apply when a contributor has licensing terms, security concerns, or privacy-related limits attached to the data. Clarus must honor those conditions and only share observations with users or partners allowed under the contributor’s agreement. Sensitive, source-limited, or conditionally shared data must carry those access rules with it so it is not exposed more widely than permitted. Clarus should carry the restriction metadata forward with the observation wherever it goes, including edits, history records, exports, and any derivative products. If a derived product includes restricted source data, then that restriction should propagate to the output unless the contributor’s terms explicitly allow broader reuse. Downstream users should never be able to separate the data from its sharing conditions. If Clarus can’t guarantee that a history entry or export will honor the limit, it should not produce that output in a way that exposes the restricted content. Additionally, anything involving credentials, internal system details, or sensitive operational data should be treated as restricted, logged access carefully, and not exposed in normal data views or exports. Clarus should treat the restriction as part of the data itself, not as separate paperwork. Every observation, history record, export, and derived output keeps the most restrictive applicable sharing rule attached to it. If a downstream system combines restricted data with less restricted data, the combined result should inherit the stricter rule unless the restricted portion has been removed or explicitly reapproved for broader sharing. The safe default is that restrictions always follow the data wherever it goes.

slots.value: Day-to-day upkeep should sit with the operations or support team for monitoring, routine fixes, user support, and environment maintenance; the program team should retain ownership of policy decisions, major changes, data governance, and anything affecting core business rules or interagency agreements. Vendor-hosted pieces or external data feeds may have shared ownership, but accountability must remain clear. Routine incidents like failed feeds, stuck jobs, display issues, and user access problems should be handled by operations first if they can be resolved without changing business rules or data governance. Issues that affect the meaning of the data, quality-control logic, retention behavior, or a cross-agency integration should be escalated to the program team or relevant owner. Public-facing availability, data integrity, and risks of users making the wrong operational decision require quick escalation even if operations can apply a temporary workaround. sections.section_content: Business Rules, Standards, and Delivery Constraints

topics.topic_content: Rules governing acceptance and classification of observations

slots.key: Observation acceptance criteria
slots.value: Accept and distinguish raw observations, quality-controlled observations, and derived conditions or alerts; labels must clearly indicate whether data came straight from the sensor, was checked or corrected, or is an interpreted result meant for action. Observation records should at minimum include the source, time of observation, location, and observation type or parameter, plus a unique record identifier for tracking through collection, quality control, and sharing. If available, site or sensor ID should also be carried through. For research-contributor data, require clear provenance, methods, and known limitations; label observations so it is obvious they came from a research source and whether they have been validated, are experimental, or are only suitable for informational use. If the data is meant to support road safety or forecasting, contributors should qualify it with enough context that users do not mistake a study dataset for an operational sensor feed. If the method or quality cannot be verified, the data may still be accepted but should be clearly flagged. Follow-up should be triggered when issues start affecting trust or operational usefulness, including repeated bad quality flags, long stretches of missing data, metadata gaps that prevent users from interpreting the observation correctly, or poor integration that causes delays, duplicates, or makes the source hard to compare with others. Recurring issues may be tolerated only as a temporary exception if the source still provides unique value, the problems are clearly documented, and there is an agreed plan to fix them so known problems do not become permanent. If a research observation has been checked against Clarus quality rules and the source and method are reasonably clear, it can be labeled as usable for operations. If we can’t fully verify the method or quality, then it should still be accepted but clearly marked as informational or experimental so users know not to rely on it the same way. At a minimum, show where it came from, when it was collected, what kind of observation it is, and any validation status or limitations known; if provenance is incomplete, that uncertainty should be visible rather than hidden.

Data-sharing policy restrictions
slots.value: Clarus should treat restrictions as part of the data itself, not as separate paperwork. Every observation, history record, export, and derived output keeps the most restrictive applicable sharing rule attached to it. If a downstream system combines restricted data with less restricted data, the combined result should inherit the stricter rule, unless the restricted portion has been removed or explicitly reapproved for broader sharing. The safe default is that restrictions always follow the data wherever it goes.

revisions.new_value: Clarus should honor contributor licensing terms, security concerns, and privacy-related limits on observation data, and only share an observation with users or partners who are allowed to receive it under the contributor’s agreement. If no special restriction applies, the default should be broad sharing for transportation and research use. Sensitive, source-limited, or conditionally shared data must carry its access rules with it so it is not exposed more widely than permitted.

slots.key: Audit log content and security alerting
slots.value: Keep audit logs for important operational and security actions, including data submissions, QC changes, administrative updates, access to sensitive records, and failed login or authorization attempts; logs should be sufficient to reconstruct who did what and when; suspicious activity should be alerted to system administrators and security staff. Anything tied to a security incident, suspected misuse, or an active investigation should be retained longer and restricted much more tightly than routine operational logs. For validated or corrected observations, preserve the original source and unique record ID exactly as received, and keep both the original and corrected versions along with who or what made the change and when it happened; corrected identifiers must stay linked to the original observation to preserve chain of custody. Sensitive access, including credentials or internal system details, should be logged carefully. For restricted observations, also record who accessed the data, when, from where if available, what action they took, and whether anything was exported or forwarded.

slots.value: Clarus should accept observations at whatever handoff point the contributor can support reliably, with preference for the most direct path that still preserves quality and traceability. A direct agency transfer is ideal when the agency can provide clean, timely data; vendor-managed feeds or local staging steps are acceptable when needed to normalize or validate data before it reaches Clarus. Unnecessary manual handling should be avoided, and setups that obscure data provenance or whether data was altered should be avoided. In speed-focused deployments, favor the simplest reliable setup; where data quality is a bigger concern, a staging or validation step may be worth the extra complexity.

slots.key: Cutover coexistence and legacy fallback timing

For anything affecting shared data or reporting, a clear cutoff date approved by the program team is required so people are not updating two systems indefinitely. Fallback to the legacy process is justified only if Clarus has a serious outage, a data integrity problem, or a failed integration that prevents reliable use for the affected workflow; if the issue is limited and can be patched quickly, operations should use a temporary workaround instead. If the problem is affecting safety-related operations or multiple users at once, that’s enough evidence to move fast rather than wait.

slots.key: Primary user tasks for finding and interpreting data
slots.value: Users need to distinguish raw observations from quality-controlled observations and from derived conditions or alerts, and tell road condition reports apart from weather observations and QC outcomes such as rejected, flagged, or verified so they can interpret what the data means for operational action. Success is judged by whether the data is timely, usable, traceable, trusted enough for operational users to support decisions, and—when thresholds are involved—kept in the system but shown with lower confidence, special status, or lower prominence rather than rejected outright, unless the value is clearly invalid (e.g. bad format or physically impossible).

slots.key: Filtering and visualization needs
slots.value: Search and visualization should respect the same access restrictions as the underlying observations, so users only see what they’re allowed to see. Filters by type, source, location, time range, confidence, and quality status are fine, and the interface should clearly indicate when a result is estimated, stale, incomplete, unverified, aggregated, or derived. Low-confidence or unverified data should not be presented as confirmed ground truth, and aggregated or derived views should be labeled so users understand they are seeing a summary rather than the raw observation. In result rows or map views, these states should be made obvious with a visible label and, where possible, a simple status indicator; users should not have to infer them from a hidden field or a download.

slots.value: The work feels complete when the core observation flow is stable and the main stakeholder groups can use it without a lot of manual intervention; follow-up is still needed if there are recurring quality issues, missing metadata, or sources that are not yet well integrated. topics.topic_content: Reliability, fault handling, and recovery of observation services

slots.key: Failure handling for missing or delayed feeds
slots.value: Fail gracefully and keep accepting whatever data can still come through rather than stopping everything; queue or hold incoming observations if possible during a handoff problem or interruption. Late reports should still be accepted if they are within the allowed window and clearly marked as late; missing reports should be treated as visible gaps rather than silently filled in.

slots.key: Recovery point and recovery time expectations
slots.value: Resume processing once the connection or downstream service comes back; prioritize minimizing delay and avoiding data loss, especially during active weather or road incidents. If the interruption is brief and Clarus can safely hold incoming observations without overflow or data loss, it should keep buffering and then resume automatically once the connection is restored. If the outage is longer or the backlog starts to threaten capacity, it should switch into a controlled recovery mode so operators can intervene without losing the most important data.

slots.key: Follow-up triggers for incomplete observation service maturity
slots.value: Recurring quality issues, missing metadata, or sources that are not yet well integrated should trigger follow-up when they start affecting trust or operational usefulness, such as repeated bad quality flags, long stretches of missing data, metadata gaps that prevent users from interpreting the observation correctly, or poor integration that causes delays, duplicates, or makes the source hard to compare with others. Some recurring issues may be tolerated temporarily if the source is still providing unique value and the problems are clearly documented, but only as a temporary exception with an agreed fix plan so that known problems do not become the permanent state.

slots.key: Missing or unavailable source record handling for drill-down
slots.value: Show a clear message that the raw observation can’t be retrieved right now, include the reason if known (for example archived, deleted, or temporarily offline), preserve the summary view and any safe context, route archived records to the archive only if the user is allowed to access it there, and for temporary unavailability let the user retry later. Missing, archived, or temporarily unavailable source records should remain reachable from the summary for as long as the summary or derived view is retained, because users still need the provenance trail; Clarus should show that the source existed and how it was used, only opening the raw record when it is actually available and the user is permitted. The missing/archived/unavailable status should not automatically remove the derived or historical view, but the summary should clearly indicate that the underlying source is not presently accessible. This reachability is limited by retention and legal-hold rules: if the raw record is deleted or retention-expired, the pointer should degrade to an auditable reference showing the source is no longer retrievable rather than preserving a live link forever; provenance metadata may be retained only as allowed, and access must follow the current retention, archive, and authorization status.

slots.key: Escalation rules for routine incidents and data-impacting issues
slots.value: Operations should handle routine incidents first, such as failed feeds, stuck jobs, display issues, and user access problems, as long as they can be resolved without changing business rules or data governance. Anything affecting data meaning, quality-control logic, retention behavior, or a cross-agency integration should be escalated to the program team or relevant owner. Issues affecting public-facing availability, data integrity, or the risk of users making the wrong operational decision should be escalated quickly even if operations can apply a temporary workaround. Operations handles restoration and triage, while the program team owns policy, exceptions, and lasting change. Immediate escalation is also required if the incident could corrupt or misrepresent observations, break a quality-control rule, expose restricted data, affect multiple agencies at once, is recurring, not well understood, or requires a policy exception. Fallback to the legacy process is justified for a serious Clarus outage, a data integrity problem, or a failed integration that prevents reliable use for the affected workflow, especially when users would otherwise be making decisions on bad or incomplete data. The fallback decision should be approved by the program lead or designated business owner, with operations recommending it based on the incident; for anything broader than a local issue, the affected agency or data owner should also be involved before the fallback path is declared active. Immediate fallback is justified when Clarus is unavailable, producing clearly incorrect observations, or the QC and integration flow is failing in a way that would mislead operators. If the problem is affecting safety-related operations or multiple users at once, that’s enough evidence to move fast rather than wait. In a true emergency, the program lead or business owner can approve the switch first and notify the affected agency or data owner right after. For a non-urgent issue, they should be consulted before the switch, especially if the fallback changes who is responsible for the data or how it’s reported.

topics.topic_content: Protection of contributor systems, credentials, and sensitive data

slots.key: Authentication and authorization controls
slots.value: Credentials must be protected and access limited to the right roles when agencies or vendors are sending data into Clarus, when users access operational dashboards or downloads, and when administrative changes are made to sources or quality-control settings.

revisions.new_value: Credentials must be protected and access limited to the right roles when agencies or vendors are sending data into Clarus, when users access operational dashboards or downloads, and when administrative changes are made to sources or quality-control settings.

slots.key: Protection of nonpublic or restricted datasets
slots.value: Sensitive data protection is needed for feeds containing anything not meant for broad distribution, contributor account details, internal network information, and unpublished operational data, with controls so only authorized users and systems can see or change it. Data with licensing terms, security concerns, privacy-related limits, or other source/contributor-specific sharing restrictions must be shared only with users or partners allowed under the contributor’s agreement, and those access rules must travel with the data so it is not exposed more widely than permitted. Clarus should carry the restriction metadata forward with the observation wherever it goes, including edits, history records, exports, and any derivative products. If a derived product includes restricted source data, then that restriction should propagate to the output unless the contributor’s terms explicitly allow broader reuse. Downstream users should never be able to separate the data from its sharing conditions, and if Clarus cannot guarantee that a history entry or export will honor the limit, it should not produce that output in a way that exposes the restricted content. Clarus should treat the restriction as part of the data itself, not as separate paperwork. Every observation, history record, export, and derived output keeps the most restrictive applicable sharing rule attached to it. If a downstream system combines restricted data with less restricted data, the combined result should inherit the stricter rule, unless the restricted portion has been removed or explicitly reapproved for broader sharing. The safe default is that restrictions always follow the data wherever it goes.

slots.key: Audit logging and security monitoring needs
slots.value: Keep audit logs for important operational and security actions, especially data submissions, QC changes, administrative updates, access to sensitive records, and failed login or authorization attempts. Logs should be sufficient to reconstruct who did what and when. For restricted observations, logs should record who accessed the data, when, from where if available, what action they took, and whether anything was exported or forwarded. Suspicious activity should at least be alerted to system administrators and security staff. Retention period is not yet confirmed and may depend on policy or compliance needs. Security incident, suspected misuse, or active investigation logs should be retained longer and restricted much more tightly than routine operational logs. Records containing sensitive source details, credentials, or information that could expose weaknesses in a network or system should be excluded from normal visibility and handled separately with access controls. Access to restricted audit details must be limited to authorized staff for a specific non-routine purpose, with a clear role or approval path for investigation, oversight, or troubleshooting, and access to those details must be recorded. Audit details exports should go only to people or systems with an approved need, usually tied to a named investigation, oversight, or support case rather than general distribution; the export should be limited to the smallest necessary set of records and fields, with redaction of credentials, personal identifiers, internal addresses, and anything else not required. An emergency or exception path is allowed only for a documented incident or legal obligation with authorized approver signoff, and any broader use must be temporary, logged, and returned to restricted handling once the immediate need ends.

slots.key: Data handling rules for missing, inconsistent, and non-comparable observations
slots.value: Preserve missing or inconsistent status instead of forcing a value; clearly indicate when condition codes cannot be cleanly mapped across sources; normalize units where possible while keeping original meaning traceable; do not imply equivalence across sources without a defined conversion or mapping. Normalize only when the underlying meaning is truly the same, such as shared unit, common timestamp basis, or a standard observation type that maps cleanly across contributors. If source method, calibration, or reporting context differs in a way that could change interpretation, preserve the original value and carry a flag or metadata showing it is not directly comparable. When in doubt, keep the source detail intact and let downstream users decide whether to compare it. If a report arrives late, Clarus should still accept it if it’s within the allowed window and clearly mark it as late. If a report is missing, Clarus should treat it as a visible gap rather than silently filling it in. If reporting periods overlap, Clarus should detect the overlap and either reconcile it according to source rules or flag it for review so duplicate or conflicting records are not treated as separate truth. Clarus should preserve the original source and unique record ID exactly as received so the record can always be traced back. If a value is corrected during validation, the system should keep both the original and the corrected version along with who or what made the change and when it happened. Time, location, observation type, and any site or sensor ID should be carried forward unless they are clearly wrong or missing, and then replaced only through an auditable correction process. Any corrected identifiers should stay linked to the original observation so the chain of custody is preserved.

slots.value: During cutover, Clarus should become the system of record as soon as the migrated data and integrations are validated for that area. Legacy processes may stay available briefly as a fallback. The old process can run in parallel only until the team is confident Clarus is producing the same or better results and users have been trained. There is no fixed universal time limit; the cutoff should be based on readiness, risk, and the specific workflow. For anything affecting shared data or reporting, a clear cutoff date approved by the program team is required so people are not updating two systems indefinitely. Switch back to the legacy process only for a serious Clarus outage, a data integrity problem, or a failed integration that prevents reliable use for the affected workflow. If the issue is limited and can be patched quickly, operations should use a temporary workaround instead. Fallback is justified if users would otherwise be making decisions on bad or incomplete data. The decision should be approved by the program lead or designated business owner, with operations recommending it based on the incident. For anything broader than a local issue, the affected agency or data owner should also be kept in the loop before the fallback path is declared active. Immediate fallback is justified when Clarus is unavailable, producing clearly incorrect observations, or the QC and integration flow is failing in a way that would mislead operators. If the problem is affecting safety-related operations or multiple users at once, that’s enough evidence to move fast rather than wait. In a true emergency, the program lead or business owner can approve the switch first and notify the affected agency or data owner right after. For a non-urgent issue, they should be consulted before the switch, especially if the fallback changes who is responsible for the data or how it’s reported.
